children: In its October 28, 2026 judgment, the court also reiterated that issues not raised before the court while challenging an arbitral award under Section 34 cannot subsequently be introduced in an appeal under Section 37.

The Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal filed by the Chief Electoral Officer and another authority, upholding an arbitral award of Rs 1,00,28,788 in favour of Mahlakshmi Light House over the supply of tentage, furniture and electrical items during the 1999 Lok Sabha elections.

A Division Bench of Justice Avneesh Jhingan and Justice Shail Jain held that the arbitrator’s findings were based on a plausible assessment of the evidence and did not suffer from perversity or patent illegality warranting interference under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

In its October 28, 2026 judgment, the court also reiterated that issues not raised before the court while challenging an arbitral award under Section 34 cannot subsequently be introduced in an appeal under Section 37.

The dispute arose after the authorities awarded Mahlakshmi Light House a contract on August 9, 1999, to supply tentage, furniture and electrical items on hire for the Karol Bagh and Outer Delhi parliamentary constituencies during the Lok Sabha elections.
The contractor raised bills of Rs 19,98,426 for Karol Bagh and Rs 80,30,654 for Outer Delhi, aggregating to Rs 1,00,29,080.
The authorities alleged that the bills were inflated and issued a show-cause notice on March 31, 2000, citing the failure to submit daily challans verified by the respective Returning Officers.

Invoking arbitration, the contractor raised claims amounting to Rs 1,00,28,788. The arbitrator awarded the entire claimed amount, along with interest at 9% per annum on Rs 15,22,772 from February 2000 until payment, post-award interest at the same rate in the event of non-payment within two months, and costs of Rs 2 lakh.
The authorities challenged the award under Section 34 of the Act.
After the Single Judge dismissed their objections on May 2, 2017, they approached the Division Bench under Section 37.

The appellants argued that Clause 19 of the agreement made payment conditional upon daily submission of challans, physical verification of the tentage before dismantling, and scrutiny and approval of the bills by the competent authority.

They contended that the arbitrator had failed to adequately consider the Finance Department’s objections alleging inflated bills and the departmental inquiry reports concerning the officials involved.
The respondent countered that the arguments now advanced had not been pressed before the Single Judge and that the arbitrator had adequately considered the objections.
It also maintained that the challans had been submitted and the supplied items physically verified by the Returning Officers.

The Division Bench noted that, during the Section 34 proceedings, the authorities had pressed only one ground concerning the alleged inflation of bills and the departmental inquiry findings. No other issue was pressed.
The court observed that the appellants had not pleaded that the issues actually pressed before the Single Judge had been left undecided.
It held that issues not raised in the Section 34 proceedings could not be introduced for the first time in an appeal under Section 37.
On the merits, the court rejected the contention that the arbitrator had ignored the Finance Department’s objections.
The Bench noted that the Returning Officers of the two constituencies had testified that the bills were signed after physical verification of the supplied items.
Other officials also supported the evidence concerning verification of the challans.

The court further observed that the departmental scrutiny began in July 2000, after the tentage structures had been dismantled, whereas the physical verification by the Returning Officers had taken place before dismantling.

It also noted that a subsequent report dated October 24, 2001, recommended a deduction of Rs 12,95,221 for the Karol Bagh constituency, but the comments recorded on the report stated, “I hope the calculations are correct.”
The Bench also considered the departmental inquiry reports dated January 24, 2006, and February 15, 2006, concerning two officials.

It noted that the allegations against one official were not proved, while the report concerning the other had not been placed before the arbitrator. Further, the reports did not concern the Returning Officers who had physically verified the challans and bills.

Relying on the principles governing judicial review of arbitral awards, the court held that the assessment of the evidence and the determination of the quantum of evidence required to establish a claim fell within the arbitrator’s domain.

The Bench referred to the Supreme Court’s decision in State of Rajasthan v. Ferro Concrete Construction (P) Ltd., which recognised the arbitrator’s authority to assess the evidence supporting a claim, while distinguishing cases where an award is made without any supporting evidence.
The court acknowledged that patent illegality and perversity may justify setting aside an award under Section 34, referring to the Supreme Court decisions in Associate Builders v.
Delhi Development Authority and Delhi Airport Metro Express Private Limited v. Delhi Metro Rail Corporation Ltd.
However, it concluded that the arbitrator’s view was plausible and suffered from no factual or legal error, much less perversity, warranting judicial interference.
Accordingly, the Division Bench dismissed the appeal and upheld the arbitral award.
Advocates Dhananjaya Mishra, Navneet Dogra and Bhargav Verma appeared for the appellants.
Senior Advocate Suhail Dutt appeared for Mahlakshmi Light House, along with Advocates Saran Suri, Ruchi Jain, Azhar Alam, Nagashree N. Sharma and Aman Yadav.
